question: What is the correct EMMO class for a scanning electron microscope observation? Should I use 'Measurement' or 'Observation', and how do they differ?
I want to record that my tensile test followed DIN EN ISO 6892-1. How do I attach a standard or protocol to a process description in RDF?
model_answer:
To attach a standard or protocol such as DIN EN ISO 6892-1 to a process description in RDF, you can use the property "has standard" from the StahlDigital Process Ontology.
The class for standards is: https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/Standard
The property to attach a standard to a process is: https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/hasStandard
You would describe your process as an instance of a process class and then link it using the "has standard" property to the standard (DIN EN ISO 6892-1) you want to indicate it follows.
Example RDF snippet in Turtle (ttl) syntax:
ttl

@prefix ex: <http://example.org/myOntology#> .
@prefix proc: <https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/> .

ex:MyTensileTestProcess a proc:Process ;
    proc:hasStandard ex:DIN_EN_ISO_6892_1 .

ex:DIN_EN_ISO_6892_1 a proc:Standard ;
    rdfs:label "DIN EN ISO 6892-1" .
Here, ex:MyTensileTestProcess is your process individual, and ex:DIN_EN_ISO_6892_1 represents the standard followed. The property proc:hasStandard relates the process to the standard. You can replace ex: with your actual namespace and add further details as needed.

question: After rolling, my copper sheet has a grain size of 15 µm measured by EBSD. How do I link the microstructure characterization to the manufacturing process that caused it?
model_answer:
To link the microstructure characterization such as the grain size of 15 µm measured by EBSD to the manufacturing process that caused it, you can use concepts from the ontologies as follows:
Manufacturing Process: You can represent the manufacturing process that caused the microstructure characteristics using the class "ManufacturingProcess" (https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/ManufacturingProcess).
Microstructure: The microstructure of the material, which includes features like grain size, can be represented using the class "Microstructure" (https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/Microstructure). This class captures the morphological aspects of the material portion of matter.
Grain Size: The specific microstructure characteristic "grain size" can be expressed with the class "GrainSize" (https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/GrainSize).
Linkage Property: Although a specific property linking the manufacturing process to the microstructure was not found explicitly, you can express that a manufacturing process "has produced" or "hasEffectOn" a microstructure with a certain grain size, or use a property like "hasMicrostructureModel" (https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/hasMicrostructureModel) if you have a microstructure model.
Example RDF snippet:
ttl

@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .
@prefix po: <https://w3id.org/steel/ProcessOntology/> .

ex:RollingProcess a po:ManufacturingProcess .

ex:CopperSheet a po:Microstructure ;
    po:hasMicrostructureModel ex:EBSDGrainSizeMeasurement .

ex:EBSDGrainSizeMeasurement a po:GrainSize ;
    ex:hasValue "15"^^xsd:float ;
    ex:hasUnit "micrometer" .

ex:RollingProcess ex:hasEffectOn ex:CopperSheet .
This way you represent the manufacturing process (rolling) and link it to the microstructure characterization (grain size) of the copper sheet. Let me know if you want more detailed properties or specific ontology terms for quantities and units.

question: I have a dataset of 50 fatigue test cycles for a steel specimen. Should each cycle be its own process individual, or should I use a collection class? What does EMMO suggest?
model_answer:
In EMMO, a fatigue test cycle can be modeled as a process. The class for process is https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_43e9a05d_98af_41b4_92f6_00f79a09bfce, which is a subclass of Persistence, and represents occurrences with temporal parts.
For representing multiple cycles, there is a Collection class in EMMO: https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_2d2ecd97_067f_4d0e_950c_d746b7700a31. This class represents causal clusters and can be used to group multiple members with properties like "Has Member" to link members to the collection.
Therefore, if you have 50 fatigue test cycles, you can either:
Represent each cycle as its own individual instance of Process (https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_43e9a05d_98af_41b4_92f6_00f79a09bfce).
Or create one Collection of fatigue test cycles as an instance of Collection (https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_2d2ecd97_067f_4d0e_950c_d746b7700a31) and use the "Has Member" property to include each cycle as a member of the collection.
Using a Collection to group the cycles is a recommended pattern when representing multiple related process instances as a whole. Each cycle as a process individual represents detailed temporal parts.
Example RDF snippet in Turtle for using Collection:
turtle

@prefix emmo: <https://w3id.org/emmo#> .

:fatigueTestCycles a emmo:Collection ;
    emmo:HasMember :cycle1, :cycle2, :cycle3, ... , :cycle50 .

:cycle1 a emmo:Process .
:cycle2 a emmo:Process .
# etc.
This way, you model the set of 50 cycles as a collection, while each cycle is separately identified as a process. This approach aligns with EMMO principles. Let me know if you want examples for process individuals too.

question: How do I express that two different labs measured the same property on the same batch of material but got slightly different values? Which BFO or EMMO concepts handle inter-lab provenance?
My corrosion experiment produced mass-loss data over time. How do I model a time series of measurements — do I create one measurement individual per time point, or use a dataset class?
model_answer:
For modeling your corrosion experiment mass-loss data as a time series, the PMD Core Ontology defines "time series" (https://w3id.org/pmd/co/PMD_0000992) as a 1-D information content entity consisting of a sequence of data points collected at successive time intervals for analyzing temporal trends.
You could model your data using a time series class instance that represents the overall sequence of mass-loss measurements over time. Each measurement at a specific time point can be represented as an individual data point within that time series entity.
Regarding individual measurements, the Elementary Multiperspective Material Ontology (EMMO) defines a "Measurement Result" (https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_0f6f0120_c079_4d95_bb11_4ddee05e530e) as the result of a measurement, possibly including relevant details like uncertainties.
So, you have two options:
Create one measurement individual per time point (each being a Measurement Result) and then relate them sequentially or as members of the time series.
Use a time series class instance to hold the entire ordered collection of data points.
In practice, a hybrid approach is often used where the time series entity groups multiple measurement individuals each representing the mass-loss at a particular time.

question: I want to assert that specimen A and specimen B were cut from the same parent sample. Is there an EMMO or BFO relation for physical derivation / part-of at the material level?
model_answer:
For asserting that specimen A and specimen B were cut from the same parent sample, you can use the following relations from BFO and EMMO ontologies:
BFO has the property "part of" (http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000050). This relation is a generic part-whole relation with no specified domain or range. It can be used to state that an entity (e.g., specimen) is part of a whole (e.g., parent sample).
EMMO provides a more specialized property "Has Spatial Part" (https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_dc57d998_23db_4d8e_b2cd_f346b195b846) with domain "CausalSystem". This property indicates a proper part of a whole where the parts cover the full temporal extension of the whole within a spatial interval. It is a subproperty of "hasNonTemporalPart," linking to the EMMO part hierarchy.
If you want to specifically assert that specimen A and B are parts spatially derived from the same parent sample, EMMO's "Has Spatial Part" is a strong candidate. If you prefer a more general relation, BFO's "part of" could be used.
Here is an example of usage in RDF Turtle syntax with BFO's "part of":
ttl

@prefix ex: <http://example.org/specimens/> .
@prefix bfo: <http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_> .

ex:SpecimenA bfo:0000050 ex:ParentSample .
ex:SpecimenB bfo:0000050 ex:ParentSample .
Alternatively, using EMMO's "Has Spatial Part":
ttl

@prefix ex: <http://example.org/specimens/> .
@prefix emmo: <https://w3id.org/emmo#> .

ex:ParentSample emmo:EMMO_dc57d998_23db_4d8e_b2cd_f346b195b846 ex:SpecimenA, ex:SpecimenB .
Let me know if you want me to help with more detailed assertions or example usage!

My agent should distinguish between a 'test coupon' (the physical object), the 'material' it is made of, and the 'role' it plays in a test. Which BFO + EMMO classes cover object, material, and role respectively?
model_answer:
For your agent to distinguish between a 'test coupon' as a physical object, the material it is made of, and the role it plays in a test, here are the relevant classes from BFO and EMMO ontologies:
Object (the physical entity, e.g., the test coupon):
BFO class: bfo
(http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000030)
It is a subclass of material entity.
Definition: An object is a material entity which manifests causal unity and is of a type whose instances are maximal relative to the causal unity manifested.
Material (the substance the object is made of):
EMMO class: emmo
(https://w3id.org/emmo#EMMO_4207e895_8b83_4318_996a_72cfb32acd94)
It is a subclass of OrdinaryMatter and Substance.
EMMO description: Matter composed of only matter particles, excluding anti-matter particles; a composite physical object made of fermions (i.e. having mass and occupying space).
Role (the function or part the object plays in a test):
BFO class: bfo
(http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000023)
It is a subclass of realizable entity.
Definition: A role is a realizable entity that exists because there is some single bearer in special physical, social, or institutional circumstances, such that the bearer does not have to be in that role, and if the role ceases to exist, the physical make-up of the bearer is not changed.
Usage example in Turtle (ttl) syntax:
ttl

@prefix bfo: <http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_> .
@prefix emmo: <https://w3id.org/emmo#> .
@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .

ex:TestCoupon a bfo:object ;
    bfo:hasMaterial ex:SteelMaterial ;
    bfo:hasRole ex:TestSampleRole .

ex:SteelMaterial a emmo:Material .

ex:TestSampleRole a bfo:role .
This structure clearly separates the physical object, the material it is made of, and the role it plays in an experimental context. Let me know if you want further examples or assistance!
